events.text: {npc}, a young keeper of the harbour shrine with salt in {his} hair and a basket of unburnt prayer-papers, intercepts you at the shrine steps. "I burn the village's prayers every dawn," {he} says. "The ash falls on the water. It never rises. I have asked three priests why and they all changed the subject."

effects.log: You walk to the quay's end together. The grey film lies on the water, perfectly still.

choices.text: Ask what the three priests said

effects.log: "Nothing," {npc} says. "They said nothing three different ways."

choices.text: Say prayers fall where gods will

effects.log: {npc} nods politely and takes the basket away.

events.text: You and {npc} burn the dawn's prayers at the end of the quay and watch the ash. It does not rise toward the domain above. It falls onto the water and lies there, a still grey film that drifts, slowly and deliberately, toward one pile of the quay. {npc} points. "There," {he} says. "It always goes there."

choices.text: Touch the film with a fingertip

effects.log: It is cold and faintly warm at once, like a held breath.
{npc} counts it out: every morning for as long as {he} has kept the shrine.

events.text: Under the last pile of the quay, in the cold green dark, sits a clay jar bound with seven knots and stamped with the temple's own seal. The sea around it is dead still. {npc} stays on the quay holding the lamp and the rope. "Someone put this here," {he} calls down. "On purpose. Carefully."

choices.text: Press your palm to the jar

effects.log: It hums faintly, like a sleeper breathing. The knots are old rope, not new.
You surface and tell {npc} only what you saw. The jar stays exactly as it was.

events.text: The harbour priest pours tea for you and {npc} with hands that will not keep still. When you speak of the jar the cup goes over. "The tide god swamped a boat once over a late offering," the priest says. "We sealed the god asleep. We promised to wake it when we were ready. We were never ready. Please do not wake it."

effects.log: You thank the priest for the tea. {npc} walks out beside you in silence.
The priest looks at you as if you were the first kind thing in years.

events.text: On the quay at low tide, with {npc} beside you and the village watching, you say it: the tide god was sealed asleep in a jar, and every prayer for generations has fallen on a sleeper. The old priest weeps. Then {npc} steps forward, takes the first rope knot in two hands, and looks to you.

choices.text: Wake the god gently, with the whole village praying

mem.note: woke the tide god with you

effects.log: The seals come undone one by one. The water rises, soft as a yawn, and the village's prayers finally have somewhere to go.

choices.text: Take the matter to the Heavenly Court

effects.log: The Court sends a warden to wake the god with proper rites. Your name is read in the harbour for a season.

events.text: Your answer goes round the harbour before noon, and it is wrong. The villagers turn on the Ministry's tax-man, and an innocent clerk is shouted off the quay. {npc} finds you after. "It was not that," {he} says quietly. "I swam to the jar. Nobody lost anything. Something was kept."

effects.log: You find the clerk at the inn and say you were wrong, where the harbour can hear.

choices.text: Go back to the jar and think

effects.log: You go over the knots, the seal, the film. Somewhere is what you missed.

events.text: A month of watching the ash, and the weather turns: a fog that sits on the harbour for weeks. {npc} cannot see the quay's end from the shrine. "The trail goes cold," {he} says. "We wait for a clear dawn."

effects.log: You write down everything you have so far, so the waiting loses none of it.
You walk it blind, counting piles. You will know them in the dark now.

events.text: The rope breaks as you descend, and the cold green dark takes you for a long minute. You come up scraped and coughing. {npc} hauls you out onto the quay and scolds you the whole way, with tears {he} will not admit.

effects.log: You let {him}. It is a kind of care.
You are not fine. {npc} knows it, and says nothing.

events.text: {npc}, an archivist of the Celestial Ministries with a clerk's stoop and a dry, careful voice, finds you in the reading hall and slides a single leaf across the table. "A blank page in the Book of Fates," {he} says. "Han Dal-rae, a weaver. Blank since the age of nine. And Han lives. Pages do not go blank."

effects.log: A plain weaver's page, ruled and numbered, and then simply nothing.

choices.text: Ask why {npc} brings it to you

effects.log: "Because the Ministries will not look," {npc} says. "You might."

choices.text: Say a blank page is a fault in the paper

effects.log: {npc} takes the leaf back without arguing.

events.text: The Book of Fates is chained to a lectern in the Ministries' hall, and {npc} turns its leaves with white gloves. Han Dal-rae's page is ruled, headed, numbered, and then at the age of nine it simply stops. Thirty more years should be there. {npc} runs a gloved finger down the empty ruling. "Han is alive," {he} says. "The Book says otherwise."

choices.text: Hold the page to the lamp

effects.log: No scraping, no erasing. The page was never written. Somebody took the writing away whole.
{npc} checks. All of them are full.

events.text: The clerk who last held the page is now a minor door-god of a granary in a hill-vale, and has a taste for millet wine. "That page," the door-god says, "was borrowed by a goddess of cradles. A signature that never dried. I did not ask. One does not ask a cradle-goddess why." {npc} writes it all down.

choices.text: Thank the door-god and leave a small offering

effects.log: The door-god bows. It is not often that anyone remembers the granary.

choices.text: Ask where the cradle-goddess keeps a shrine

effects.log: "Past the third ford," the door-god says. "Beside the weir."

events.text: In the cradle-goddess's shrine beside the weir, behind a screen of rushes, lies the borrowed leaf. Another page sits with it: a fate of seventy years, written fair, and the name at its head is not the weaver's but a sickly child's. {npc} stares at you. "They share it," {he} whispers. "Two lives, one page."

effects.log: You close the screen of rushes. Nobody must know yet.
{npc} folds the copy into {his} sleeve like a blade.

events.text: At the Ministries' open hearing, with {npc} beside you, you lay it out: a cradle-goddess, fearing a child would not live a year, copied the weaver's fate onto the child, and the weaver's own page went blank. Both live, in step. The hearing is silent a long moment. Then the cradle-goddess, in a hood, rises from the back and says, "I could not bear it. Do not punish them."

choices.text: Ask the Ministries to give each a page of their own

effects.log: Two new leaves are written, in two hands. The child and the weaver learn each other's names that spring.

choices.text: Let the Ministries have the credit

effects.log: The cradle-goddess is admonished lightly. The hearing names you as the reader who found the page.

events.text: Your answer goes round the Ministries' corridors, and it is the wrong one. An innocent god is called before the clerks to explain a disguise they never wore. {npc} finds you after. "It was not that," {he} says. "A hidden god leaves a page full of lies. This page was left empty on purpose."

effects.log: You go to the god in person and say you were wrong. It is accepted without warmth.

choices.text: Go back to the empty page

effects.log: Blank is also a kind of writing. You read it again.

events.text: You ask for the Book of Fates a second time in a season, and the Ministries' warden reads a rule about idle petitions. The hall is half full. {npc} goes red to the ears on your behalf. "Perhaps," {he} says, "we should have asked more quietly."

effects.log: You laugh louder than the warden. The hall forgives you.
The Ministries forget in a season. You do not.

events.text: Word gets round the Ministries that you are chasing a blank page, and the corridors enjoy it. Someone has pinned up a comic notice. {npc} sees it and takes it down with great dignity, and rather too much force.

effects.log: You laugh louder than anyone. The notice loses its sting.
Let them pin. The truth does not care who is laughing.

events.text: {npc}, an old shrine-keeper from a hill village with a stick, a shawl, and an air of having walked a long way, stops you on the road. "Every dawn we pray to a god," {he} says, "by a name nobody remembers. They say it was a kind god. You walk like the god in the old songs. Forgive an old man. Will you come and see the altar?"

effects.log: It is a long climb. {npc} talks the whole way, of winters and children and a god who never failed.

choices.text: Ask what name they pray to

effects.log: {npc} says it. It means nothing to you, and your heart turns over anyway.

choices.text: Say you are only passing through

effects.log: {npc} nods and goes on up the hill without asking again.

events.text: The hill village is small and poor, and the altar at its heart is smaller: a flat stone, a bronze bowl, a few sprigs of winter herb. A name is cut into it, in a script you can read although you were never taught it. {npc} lights the dawn incense. "Every day," {he} says. "For as long as the hill has been here."

choices.text: Lay your palm on the cut name

effects.log: The stone is warm, and for one heartbeat you are older, and kinder, and standing here at the first light.

choices.text: Let {npc} finish the dawn rite alone

effects.log: {npc} finishes it with great tenderness, as if you were watching a family at supper.

events.text: The village's oldest sing the dawn prayer for you, and it is not a petition but a lullaby: keep the children warm through the winter, keep the roofs from the snow. {npc} hums it under {his} breath. "The god kept us," {he} says. "Once. A hard winter, long ago. They say the god never asked a thing for it."

choices.text: Ask what became of the god

effects.log: "Went up," {npc} says. "Never came back down. We keep the place warm."

choices.text: Sit with the old singers a while

effects.log: You sit till the light is full. The lullaby goes round again, and you know every note.

events.text: In the Book of Fates, the god's entry is a closed leaf: ascended, then silent, the hill's faith still tied to the name like a kite string to a post. The closing date is the year before you were born. {npc} reads it twice. The last piece is not here: whoever could answer for that god has not been born yet, or has not found the hill.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to keep the entry safe

effects.log: {npc} promises to keep the copy, and the lullaby, and the altar warm. "For whoever comes asking," {he} says.

choices.text: Burn a stick of incense at the altar

effects.log: The smoke goes straight up, which the hill calls a good sign.

events.text: You are young in this life, and have never been to the hill, and still your feet know the last turn of the path. At the altar waits {npc}, who looks at you a long time. "The hill kept your place," {he} says. "I was told you would come at dawn, looking as though you were late and sorry for it. Come in. The bowl is warm."

effects.log: The smoke rises in a thin straight line. Somewhere under your ribs, an old warmth settles.
"My teacher," {npc} says. "Who was told by the teacher before. It is in the lullaby."

events.text: At dawn, at the flat stone altar, with {npc} beside you and the hill village gathered, you say it aloud: the god was you, in the life before this one. The hill kept your place by praying to your name for generations. {npc} bows low. "We were not praying to a stranger," {he} says. "Only to someone late."

choices.text: Sing the lullaby with the hill

effects.log: You sing it, badly, and the whole hill joins. The oldest villager sits down hard and weeps for joy.

choices.text: Take the hill's dawn offering as a god once did

effects.log: You accept the bowl as the hill has offered it for ages, and the village's faith comes home to you.

events.text: "A false god," you said, or "a borrowed name," and the hill hears it from a passing pilgrim before nightfall. The villagers stop singing the dawn prayer for a week. {npc} comes to you in the dark. "It was not that," {he} says quietly. "Our god is real. Our god is only late."

effects.log: You climb it again and say you were wrong, at dawn, where all can hear.

choices.text: Sit at the altar and think

effects.log: You sit with the name until the sun is up.

events.text: A season of climbing the hill and asking the old singers, and the winter closes the pass. {npc} sends word that the road is shut until spring. "The trail goes cold," the message says. "The hill will keep."

effects.log: You write down every verse of the lullaby you have, so the waiting loses none of it.

choices.text: Hum the lullaby through the snow

effects.log: You learn the tune by heart in the cold. You will not forget it.

events.text: Word gets round the pantheon that you are chasing an old altar with your own name on it, and the halls enjoy it. Someone has written a comic hymn. {npc} hears it and goes red to the ears on your behalf.

effects.log: You hum it louder than anyone. The hymn loses its sting.
Let them hum. The truth does not care who is laughing.

events.text: {npc}, a festival-warden with a ring of keys at {his} belt and a face used to crowds, catches you at the edge of a feast-day market. "One god, two feasts," {he} says. "The north holds one in spring. The south holds one in autumn. Each swears the other is a counterfeit. Both have sent me letters. I am running out of ways to be polite."

effects.log: Six letters from each province, each more indignant than the last. You find yourself smiling.
"Both claim it," {npc} says. "Both have the same founding story, word for word."

choices.text: Say gods can keep two feasts

effects.log: {npc} laughs politely and does not ask again.

events.text: The two provinces' festival calendars lie side by side on {npc}'s table. The spring feast and the autumn feast are described in near-identical words, down to the shape of the offering cakes. But the northern calendar names no lamp, and the southern one names no hearth. {npc} circles the gap. "Each half remembers only half the god," {he} says.

choices.text: Lay the calendars over each other

effects.log: The gaps fit. What one lacks, the other has. It is like a torn leaf.
{npc} writes two careful letters and promises you will hear both replies.

events.text: You and {npc} visit both altars on their own feast days, a season apart. The northern god holds a ladle and the southern god holds a lamp. Neither statue knows the other. The northern crowds sing a hearth-song, the southern a lamp-song, and when you hum them back to back they are two halves of one tune.

effects.log: The tune closes. {npc} lets out a long breath. "Oh," {he} says. "Oh, I see."
You take down both songs, word for word. A scholar would weep for the pair.

events.text: Your pantheon's archive keeps its god-rolls in a long dim hall smelling of dust and cedar. {npc} finds the entry and reads aloud a note in a faded hand: "Merged by decree: the minor gods of hearth and of lamp, to free a seat." {npc} sits down on the archive step. "A clerk," {he} says slowly. "A clerk made one god out of two."

effects.log: You copy it. The clerk has been dead a thousand years and the mistake is still working.

choices.text: Leave it as found, for now

effects.log: You do not tell either province yet. Not until you know what to ask of them.

events.text: At the border shrine where the two provinces meet for a truce, with {npc} beside you, you say it: two minor gods, hearth and lamp, were merged by a clerk's decree, and each province kept its half. Neither feast is false. Neither is whole. Both delegations are silent. Then the oldest northern priest laughs, and the oldest southern one laughs back.

choices.text: Propose one feast with two altars

effects.log: The next year the north brings its ladle and the south its lamp to the same table, and the feast is whole for the first time in a thousand years.

choices.text: Let the Heavenly Court restore the two gods

effects.log: The Court unmerges the decree. Hearth and lamp stand apart again, and the provinces thank the warden who found them.

events.text: Your answer goes round both provinces by nightfall, and it is wrong. Each hears it as an insult to its own feast; stalls are kicked over at the border market. {npc} finds you afterwards. "It was not that," {he} says quietly. "Neither feast is false. I knew it. I could not say why."

choices.text: Go and apologise at both altars

effects.log: You walk the road between them with a cake in each hand. It helps a little.

choices.text: Hold your tongue and think again

effects.log: You go over the two songs till you can hum them in your sleep.

events.text: You ask the Ministry of Rites for both provinces' registers, and the Ministry's clerks sigh. The petition is filed under idle requests. {npc} winces. "Every door you knock on remembers the knock," {he} says.

choices.text: Send an apology and a cake

effects.log: A small gift, an apology. It does not undo the cost, but it is noticed.
Some doors close. Others open. You go on.

events.text: Word gets round both provinces that you are poking at their feasts, and the markets enjoy it. A street-singer has put it in a comic song. {npc} hears it in the square and goes red to the ears on your behalf.

effects.log: You laugh louder than anyone. The song loses its sting.
Let them sing. The truth does not care who is laughing.

events.text: {npc}, an attendant of the oracle's hall with a lamp-snuffer in one hand and dark rings under {his} eyes, comes to you after the evening rites. "The oracle speaks at midnight to an empty hall," {he} says. "Answers to no question. I have been told to ignore it. I have ignored it for a year. I cannot ignore it any more."

effects.log: You sit in the dark hall together. The oracle's lamp gutters, and the air grows attentive.
"Different things," {npc} says. "Never the same thing twice. All of it sounds like asking."

choices.text: Say oracles mumble in their sleep

effects.log: {npc} nods and snuffs the lamp. You hear {him} sigh as {he} goes.

events.text: You and {npc} keep the midnight in the oracle's hall. The air thickens. The oracle, a still figure in a veil, speaks, and the echo-stone set in the floor glows faintly at each word. There is no pilgrim. There is no question. The oracle answers anyway, in a low steady voice, and {npc} writes down every word.

choices.text: Lay your palm on the echo-stone

effects.log: It is cold, and humming with a hundred half-heard voices.
{npc} writes until dawn and does not once look up.

events.text: At the echo-stone, with your ear close to the glowing floor, you listen. They are not answers. They are prayers, murmured in a dozen dialects, over and over: a harvest, a lost child, a roof for the winter. {npc} listens with you, and at last lowers {his} head. "They are asking," {he} says. "Someone is still asking."

choices.text: Write the prayers down, one by one

effects.log: You write for a night and a day. Every one is a small need, and plain.
You answer a lost-child prayer. The stone dims for a moment, as if surprised.

events.text: The temple masons keep their quarry records in a scroll-case behind the oracle's hall. {npc} finds the entry: the echo-stone was cut from the ruin of a burned shrine in a sealed domain, and carried here by pilgrims who had no altar left. {npc} reads it slowly. "They brought their altar with them," {he} says. "As a floor."

effects.log: You copy it out. The masons will not mind. They did not know what they quarried.

choices.text: Ask the masons about the pilgrims

effects.log: The masons remember a long, grey procession, and a woman who carried the stone's last corner on a bent back.

events.text: In the oracle's hall at midnight, with {npc} beside you and the lamp trimmed low, you say it plainly: the echo-stone remembers a burned shrine, and the oracle speaks the prayers of worshippers who lost their altar. The veiled figure turns its head, once, toward you. A single word comes out of the stone, clear for the first time: "Thank you."

choices.text: Promise to carry the prayers to a living altar

effects.log: You carry the prayers to the great shrine of a neighbouring domain, and its priests pledge to answer them. The echo-stone falls quiet and warm.

choices.text: Lay the case before the Heavenly Court

effects.log: The Court rules the burned shrine's worship must be answered. Your name is read in the hall of rites.

events.text: Your answer goes round the temple precinct before morning, and it is wrong. The oracle is moved to a back room "for rest"; a rival oracle is shouted at in the street. {npc} finds you. "It was not that," {he} says quietly. "The oracle is not mad. I have heard the prayers. The oracle is only listening."

choices.text: Ask for the oracle to be returned to the hall

effects.log: You speak in person to the high priest. The oracle is restored by evening.
You sit with the stone until the midnight comes round.

events.text: A season of midnights and the oracle speaks only static: a cloud of whispers without a single clear word. {npc} puts out the lamp and sits in the dark. "We wait," {he} says. "The stone speaks when it is ready."

effects.log: You write down all you have so far, so the waiting loses none of it.
Same whispers, but you begin to tell the voices apart.

events.text: The oracle's high priest hears you have been at the echo-stone and goes cold toward you. {npc} hears about it and winces. "Every door you knock on remembers the knock," {he} says.

choices.text: Bring the high priest an apology

effects.log: A small apology, quietly given. It does not undo the cost, but it is noticed.
Some doors close. Others open. You go on.

events.text: {npc}, a warden of the old Wall-Ring with keys like a harvest of iron fruit, stops you before the seal-door nobody opens. "You read the carved name without reading it," {he} says. "Your eyes did not move. Your lips did. Nobody has read that script since the door was sealed." Your own hands are suddenly cold.

effects.log: The stone is cold, and a half-memory of a very long night flickers through you.
"The ledger says one hand," {npc} says. "From inside. Nothing more."

choices.text: Say you read it by guessing

effects.log: {npc} looks at you a long time and lets you go.

events.text: Up close, the carved name on the seal-door runs in a script you read without having been taught, and your fingers know the seal's pattern before your eyes do. {npc} watches your hand trace it. "Nobody taught you that," {he} says. "It is older than the Wall-Ring."

choices.text: Trace the seal to its end

effects.log: The pattern closes on itself. It was meant to hold from the inside.
You step back. The door says nothing either. {npc} writes it all down.

events.text: The wall-wardens' ledger is chained to a stone shelf in the guardhouse. {npc} reads the page. The door was sealed from the inside, by one hand, and the hand's mark is a half-moon with a break. The warden of that age wrote in the margin: "Whoever sealed it did not ask to be let out. Do not open."

effects.log: You copy the half-moon with its break. Something in your ring finger aches.

choices.text: Ask the guardhouse who remembers the margin

effects.log: The oldest warden remembers only that the margin was written in tears.

events.text: The half-moon with a break is a scar on your own ring finger, the one you were born with. {npc} sees you cover it. The door was sealed the year before your birth. The last piece is not in this life: whoever could say what lies behind it did not come back this time to answer for it.

choices.text: Ask {npc} to keep the mark safe

effects.log: {npc} promises to keep the copy, and the page, and the door. "For whoever comes asking," {he} says.
The smoke goes straight up, which the wardens call a good sign.

events.text: You are young in this life, and have never been to the Wall-Ring, and still your feet find the seal-door in the dark. {npc} is waiting. "The ledger says you would come," {he} says. "Not to open it. To be told what is behind it. The warden before me wrote it down, and the warden before that. I will tell you, if you are ready to hear."

effects.log: You listen. What lies behind is not a monster but an hour, and you remember sealing it.
{npc} nods. "The door has waited this long," {he} says. "It can wait for your courage."

events.text: At the seal-door, with {npc} beside you and the wardens at a respectful distance, you say it: in a life before this one, you sealed your own worst hour behind the door and left your mark for a self strong enough to face it. {npc} sets down {his} keys. "Then it is not a calamity to guard," {he} says. "It is a grief to carry."

choices.text: Leave the door sealed and carry the grief

mem.note: stood at the door with you

effects.log: You lay your palm on the seal and let the memory be what it is. The door stays shut, and you walk away lighter.

choices.text: Ask the wardens to keep the door for you

effects.log: The wardens swear to keep it until you are ready. They bow as you go.

events.text: "A calamity wearing my name," you said, or "a forged seal to bind me," and the Wall-Ring is loud with it. A warden is questioned; a calamity-watcher is struck from the rolls for a week. {npc} says quietly, "The mark is yours. I have seen your hand. You know it."

choices.text: Speak for the warden before the guardhouse

effects.log: You go in person and say you were wrong. The warden is restored.

choices.text: Stand before the door and think

effects.log: You stand there till dark. The seal says nothing.

events.text: A season of asking, and the wardens' ledgers run dry. The trail ends at a guardhouse that burned down generations ago. {npc} brings you tea at the ashes. "Dead end," {he} says. "Doors are patient. So can we be."

effects.log: You write down all you have so far, so the waiting loses none of it.
Nothing new. But you know every flagstone of that floor.

events.text: Word gets round the Wall-Ring that you are chasing a sealed door with your own mark on it, and the guardhouse enjoys it. Someone has chalked a comic picture on the wall. {npc} scrubs it off with great dignity.

effects.log: You laugh louder than anyone. The picture loses its sting.
Let them chalk. The truth does not care who is laughing.

events.text: The second wrong answer is the last. {npc} does not argue with you this time. {He} only gathers up the notes and the copied pages, ties them with a prayer-cord, and puts them in your hands. "Keep these," {he} says. "Someone will finish it someday. Maybe even you."

effects.log: You keep it all. Perhaps a later life will open it.

mem.note: keeps the case for someone else

effects.log: {npc} takes it and promises to keep it for whoever comes next.

events.text: That is the second answer wrong, and the case is closed. {npc} lights a stick of incense, sets it in the ash-bowl, and watches the smoke a long while. "Some mysteries wait on a better season," {he} says. "Keep the thread. I will keep the door open a crack."

effects.log: You tie the thread around your wrist. A later life may know what to do with it.
You go, and {npc} stands at the door a long time.
